plan: 1 Samuel 30:1-31; 1 Chronicles 12:20-22; 1 Samuel 31:1-13; 1 Chronicles 10:1-14; 1 Chronicles 9:40-44; 2 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 1:1-16, 17-27

readings.title: The Amalĕqite Invasion
readings.subtitle: The adversary’s forces exploit a temporary absence, striking the unprotected families.
readings.text: [1 Samuel 30:1] And it came to be, when Daviḏ and his men came to Tsiqlaḡ, on the third day, that the Amalĕqites had invaded the South and Tsiqlaḡ, and struck <dn>את</dn> Tsiqlaḡ and burned it with fire. [2] And they took captive <dn>את</dn> the women and those who were there, from small to great. They did not kill anyone, but they led them away and went their way. [3] And Daviḏ and his men came to the city and saw it burned with fire, and their wives and their sons and their daughters had been taken captive.

readings.title: Strengthening in the Guarantee
readings.subtitle: Facing mutiny and profound grief, Daviḏ anchors his trust directly upon his Creator's authority.
readings.text: [4] And Daviḏ and the people who were with him lifted up their voices and wept, until they had no more power to weep. [5] And Daviḏ’s two wives, Aḥino‘am the Yizre‘ĕlitess, and Aḇiḡayil the widow of Naḇal the Karmelite, had been taken captive. [6] And Daviḏ was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because the being of all the people was grieved, each for his sons and his daughters. But Daviḏ strengthened himself in <dn>YeHoVaH</dn> his <dn>Elohim</dn>.

readings.title: Seeking the Divine Command
readings.subtitle: Rejecting presumption, Daviḏ utilizes the priestly garments to obtain clear operational instructions.
readings.text: [7] And Daviḏ said to Eḇyathar the priest, son of Aḥimeleḵ, “Please bring <dn>את</dn> the shoulder garment here to me.” So Eḇyathar brought the shoulder garment to Daviḏ. [8] And Daviḏ inquired of <dn>את</dn> <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>, saying, “Do I pursue this band? Do I overtake them?” And <dn>He</dn> answered him, <dq>“Pursue, for you shall certainly overtake them, and certainly rescue.”</dq> [9] So Daviḏ went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and came to the wadi Besor, where a halt was made by those who were left behind, [10] while Daviḏ pursued, he and four hundred men – for two hundred halted, who were too faint to pass over the wadi Besor.

readings.title: An Instrument of Providence
readings.subtitle: An abandoned servant of the enemy is restored with food and water, becoming the strategic guide to the marauding band.
readings.text: [11] And they found a man in the field, a Mitsrian, and took him to Daviḏ. And they gave him bread and he ate, and they let him drink water, [12] and gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his strength came back to him, for he had not eaten bread nor drunk water for three days and three nights. [13] And Daviḏ said to him, “To whom do you belong, and where are you from?” And he said, “I am a young man from Mitsrayim, servant of an Amalĕqite. And my master left me behind, for I had been sick three days. [14] “We attacked the south of the Kerĕthites and against that which belongs to Yehuḏah, and upon the south of Kalĕḇ, and we burned Tsiqlaḡ with fire.” [15] And Daviḏ said to him, “Could you bring me down to this marauding band?” And he said, “Swear to me by <dn>Elohim</dn> that you neither kill me nor surrender me into the hands of my master, then I bring you down to this marauding band.”

readings.title: Extracting the Spoil
readings.subtitle: The righteous execution of justice results in a complete restoration of families and a massive surplus of livestock.
readings.text: [16] And he brought him down and saw they were spread out over all the land, eating and drinking and celebrating, because of all the great spoil which they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Yehuḏah. [17] And Daviḏ struck <dn>את</dn> them from twilight until the evening of the next day. And none of them escaped, except four hundred young men who rode on camels and fled. [18] And Daviḏ rescued <dn>את</dn> all that the Amalĕqites had taken. Daviḏ also rescued his two wives. [19] And there was none missing to them, whether small or great, whether sons or daughters, or spoil or <dn>את</dn> whatever they had taken from them. Daviḏ recovered all. [20] Besides, Daviḏ captured <dn>את</dn> all the flocks and herds they had driven before those livestock, and they said, “This is Daviḏ’s spoil.”

readings.title: Establishing the Law of Equivalence
readings.subtitle: Daviḏ rejects the zero-sum greed of worthless men, establishing a permanent statute of equal distribution for all who support the mission.
readings.text: [21] And Daviḏ came to the two hundred men who were too faint to follow Daviḏ, who had also been left at the wadi Besor. And they went out to meet Daviḏ and to meet the people who were with him. And when Daviḏ came near the people, he greeted them. [22] And all the evil and worthless men of those who went with Daviḏ answered and said, “Because they did not go with us, we do not give them any of the spoil that we have rescued, except for every man’s wife and children, and let them take them and go.” [23] But Daviḏ said, “My brothers, do not do so with what <dn>YeHoVaH</dn> has given us, who has protected us and gave into our hand the band that came against us. [24] “And who would listen to you in this matter? For as his portion is who goes down to the battle, so is his portion who remains with the baggage, they share alike.” [25] And it came to be, from that day forward, he appointed it for a law and a right-ruling for Yisra’ĕl to this day.

readings.title: Investing the Enemy's Wealth
readings.subtitle: The recovered wealth is utilized to strengthen alliances and bless the elders of Yehuḏah across multiple cities.
readings.text: [26] And when Daviḏ came to Tsiqlaḡ, he sent some of the spoil to the elders of Yehuḏah, to his friends, saying, “Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>,” [27] to those in Bĕyth Ĕl, and to those in Ramoth of the South, and to those in Yattir, [28] and to those in Aro‘ĕr, and to those in Siphmoth, and to those in Eshtemoa, [29] and to those in Raḵal, and to those in the cities of the Yeraḥme’ĕlites, and to those in the cities of the Qĕynites, [30] and to those in Ḥormah, and to those in Korashan, and to those in Athaḵ, [31] and to those in Ḥeḇron, and to all the places where Daviḏ had gone up and down, he and his men.

readings.title: A Camp Like Elohim
readings.subtitle: Mighty men from Menashsheh recognize the transfer of authority, defecting to Daviḏ to form an apex military force.
readings.text: [20] When he went to Tsiqlaḡ, those of Menashsheh who went over to him were Aḇnah, and Yozaḇaḏ, and Yeḇiya’ĕl, and Miḵa’ĕl, and Yozaḇaḏ, and Elihu, and Tsillethai, chiefs of the thousands who were from Menashsheh. [21] And they helped Daviḏ against the raiding bands, for they were all mighty brave men, and they were commanders in the army. [22] For at that time they came to Daviḏ day by day to help him, until it was a great army, like an army of <dn>Elohim</dn>.

readings.title: The Final Stand of Sha’ul
readings.subtitle: Severely wounded and facing defeat, Sha’ul and his sons perish in battle against the uncircumcised Philistines.
readings.text: [1 Samuel 31:1] And the Philistines were fighting against Yisra’ĕl, and the men of Yisra’ĕl fled from before the Philistines, and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. [2] And the Philistines followed hard after Sha’ul and his sons. And the Philistines struck Yehonathan, and Aḇinaḏaḇ, and Malkishua, sons of Sha’ul. [3] And the battle went hard against Sha’ul, and the archers hit him, so that he was severely wounded by the archers. [4] And Sha’ul said to his armour-bearer, “Draw <dn>את</dn> your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised men come and thrust me through and roll themselves on me.” But his armour-bearer would not, for he was greatly afraid. So Sha’ul took the sword and fell on it. [5] And when his armour-bearer saw that Sha’ul was dead, he also fell on his sword, and died with him. [6] Thus Sha’ul died, and three of his sons, and his armour-bearer, also all his men, together on that day.

readings.title: The Forfeiture of the Cities
readings.subtitle: The death of the king triggers systemic collapse, allowing the enemy to inhabit the forsaken cities of Yisra’ĕl.
readings.text: [7] And they saw – the men of Yisra’ĕl who were beyond the valley, and those who were beyond the Yardĕn – that the men of Yisra’ĕl had fled and that Sha’ul and his sons were dead. So they forsook the cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

readings.title: The Boldness of Yaḇĕsh Gil‘aḏ
readings.subtitle: Despite the brutal desecration of the royal bodies, courageous men mobilize to reclaim and properly inter the fallen leadership.
readings.text: [8] And the next day it came to be, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Sha’ul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. [9] And they cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and sent word throughout the land of the Philistines, to announce it in the house of their idols and to the people. [10] And they placed his armour in the house of the Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Bĕyth Shan. [11] And the inhabitants of Yaḇĕsh Gil‘aḏ heard what the Philistines had done to Sha’ul, [12] and all the brave men arose and went all night, and took <dn>את</dn> the body of Sha’ul and <dn>את</dn> the bodies of his sons from the wall of Bĕyth Shan. And they came to Yaḇĕsh and burned them there. [13] And they took <dn>את</dn> their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree at Yaḇĕsh, and fasted for seven days.

readings.title: The Chronicler's Witness
readings.subtitle: A parallel documentation confirming the catastrophic military defeat and the systemic failure of the initial earthly king.
readings.text: [1 Chronicles 10:1] And the Philistines fought against Yisra’ĕl. And the men of Yisra’ĕl fled from before the Philistines, and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. [2] And the Philistines pursued Sha’ul and his sons, and the Philistines struck Yonathan, and Aḇinaḏaḇ, and Malkishua, sons of Sha’ul. [3] And the battle was heavy on Sha’ul. And the archers hit him, and he was wounded by the archers. [4] And Sha’ul said to his armour-bearer, “Draw <dn>את</dn> your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised ones come and abuse me.” But his armour-bearer would not, for he was much afraid, so Sha’ul took a sword and fell on it. [5] And when his armour-bearer saw that Sha’ul was dead, he also fell on his sword and died. [6] Thus Sha’ul and his three sons died, and all his house – they died together. [7] And when all the men of Yisra’ĕl who were in the valley saw that they had fled and that Sha’ul and his sons were dead, they forsook their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

readings.title: The Official Verdict on Sha’ul
readings.subtitle: The divine record definitively states the king was executed for trespassing against the Word and seeking a medium instead of YeHoVaH.
readings.text: [8] And the next day it came to be, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Sha’ul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. [9] And they stripped him and took <dn>את</dn> his head and <dn>את</dn> his armour, and sent word throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news among their idols and among the people, [10] and put his armour in the house of their mighty ones, and fastened his head in the house of Daḡon. [11] And all Yaḇĕsh Gil‘aḏ heard of all that the Philistines had done to Sha’ul, [12] and all the brave men arose and took <dn>את</dn> the body of Sha’ul and <dn>את</dn> the bodies of his sons. And they brought them to Yaḇĕsh, and buried their bones under the tamarisk tree at Yaḇĕsh, and fasted seven days. [13] Thus Sha’ul died for his trespass which he had trespassed against <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>, because he did not guard <dn>את</dn> the Word of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>, and also for asking a medium for to make inquiry, [14] and did not inquire of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>. So <dn>He</dn> put him to death, and turned the reign over to Daviḏ son of Yishai.

readings.title: The Genealogy of Yehonathan
readings.subtitle: Despite the destruction of Sha’ul's house, the precise lineage of his righteous son is carefully maintained.
readings.text: [40] And the son of Yehonathan was Meriḇ-Ba‘al, and Meriḇ-Ba‘al brought forth <dn>את</dn> Miḵah. [41] And the sons of Miḵah: Pithon, and Meleḵ, and Taḥrĕa, [42] and Aḥaz, who brought forth <dn>את</dn> Yarah; and Yarah brought forth <dn>את</dn> Alemeth, and <dn>את</dn> Azmaveth, and <dn>את</dn> Zimri. And Zimri brought forth <dn>את</dn> Motsa; [43] and Motsa brought forth <dn>את</dn> Bin‘a, and Rephayah was his son, El‘asah his son, Atsĕl his son. [44] And Atsĕl had six sons whose names were these: Azriqam, Boḵeru, and Yishma‘ĕl, and She‘aryah, and Oḇaḏyah, and Ḥanan. These were the sons of Atsĕl.

readings.title: The Laming of Mephiḇosheth
readings.subtitle: The panic following the tragic news from Yizre‘ĕl results in the permanent physical injury of Yehonathan's young heir.
readings.text: [4] Now Yehonathan, son of Sha’ul, had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Sha’ul and Yehonathan came from Yizre‘ĕl, and his nurse took <dn>את</dn> him up and fled. And it came to be, as she hurried to flee, that he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephiḇosheth.

readings.title: The Amalĕqite’s Claim
readings.subtitle: An opportunistic survivor arrives with stolen royal insignia, delivering a calculated narrative of his role in the king's demise.
readings.text: [2 Samuel 1:1] And it came to be after the death of Sha’ul, when Daviḏ had returned from striking the Amalĕqites, that Daviḏ remained two days in Tsiqlaḡ. [2] And it came to be on the third day, that see, a man came out of the camp from Sha’ul with his garments torn and dust on his head. And it came to be, when he came to Daviḏ, that he fell to the ground and did obeisance. [3] And Daviḏ said to him, “From where do you come?” And he said to him, “I have escaped from the camp of Yisra’ĕl.” [4] And Daviḏ said to him, “What was the matter? Please inform me.” And he said, “The people have fled from the battle, and also many of the people have fallen and are dead, and Sha’ul and Yehonathan his son are dead too.” [5] And Daviḏ said to the young man who informed him, “How do you know that Sha’ul and Yehonathan his son are dead?” [6] And the young man who informed him said, “By chance I was on Mount Gilboa and saw Sha’ul leaning on his spear. And see, the chariots and horsemen followed hard after him. [7] “And when he looked behind him, he saw me and called to me, and I answered, ‘Here I am.’ [8] “And he said to me, ‘Who are you?’ So I answered him, ‘I am an Amalĕqite.’ [9] “And he said to me, ‘Please stand over me and put me to death, for agony has seized me, but my life is still in me.’ [10] “So I stood beside him and put him to death, for I knew he would not live after he had fallen. And I took <dn>את</dn> the diadem that was on his head and <dn>את</dn> the bracelet that was on his arm, and have brought them here to my master.”

readings.title: Judgment upon the Self-Confessed
readings.subtitle: Operating in strict legal right-ruling, Daviḏ sentences the Amalĕqite based entirely on the testimony of his own mouth.
readings.text: [11] And Daviḏ took hold of his garments and tore them, and also all the men who were with him. [12] And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Sha’ul and for Yehonathan his son, and for the people of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn> and for the house of Yisra’ĕl, because they had fallen by the sword. [13] Then Daviḏ asked the young man who informed him, “Where are you from?” And he answered, “I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalĕqite.” [14] And Daviḏ said to him, “How was it you were not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy <dn>את</dn> the anointed of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>?” [15] And Daviḏ called one of the young men and said, “Draw near and fall on him!” And he struck him so that he died. [16] And Daviḏ said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth has witnessed against you, saying, ‘I myself have put to death <dn>את</dn> the anointed of <dn>YeHoVaH</dn>.’ ”

readings.title: The Song of the Bow
readings.subtitle: Daviḏ composes a profound public lamentation, honoring the strength of his fallen adversary and the unprecedented love of his covenant brother.
readings.text: [17] Then Daviḏ lamented with this lamentation over Sha’ul and over Yehonathan his son, [18] and he ordered “The Bow” to be taught to the children of Yehuḏah. See, it is written in the Book of Yashar: [19] “The splendour of Yisra’ĕl Is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! [20] “Declare it not in Gath, Proclaim it not in the streets of Ashqelon, Lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, Lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. [21] “Mountains of Gilboa! No dew or rain be upon you, Nor fields of offerings. For there the shield of the mighty lay rejected, The shield of Sha’ul, not anointed with oil. [22] “From the blood of the slain, From the fat of the mighty, The bow of Yehonathan did not turn back, And the sword of Sha’ul did not return empty. [23] “Sha’ul and Yehonathan were beloved And pleasant in their lives, And in their death they were not parted. They were swifter than eagles, They were stronger than lions. [24] “Daughters of Yisra’ĕl – weep over Sha’ul, Who wrapped you in scarlet, with finery; Who decked your robes with ornaments of gold. [25] “How the mighty have fallen In the midst of the battle! Yehonathan was slain in your high places. [26] “I am distressed for you, my brother Yehonathan. You have been very pleasant to me. Your love to me was wondrous, Surpassing the love of women. [27] “How the mighty have fallen, And the weapons of battle perish!”
